1.0.0: First release. Checks the Wiki for pack updates, verifies the download by SHA-256, backs up your mods before applying an update, and can open the official Minecraft Launcher for you. Automatic self-update is not yet included in 1.0 — check the Wiki for new launcher versions manually.
1.1.0: Fixes a bug in 1.0.0 where clicking Update could report success without actually replacing the mod files in your pack's mods folder. Update now verifies the files it placed are really on disk before reporting success, and removes old version-stamped mod jars that a new version replaces. Also includes a redesigned Home/Settings/Log interface. If your pack folder was last updated by 1.0.0, the first update on 1.1.0 may leave one old-versioned jar behind for one cycle — see the launcher guide's "Confirming an update actually applied" section.
1.2.0: Fixes a bug where the "Install updates automatically" setting on the Settings screen was saved but never actually used — turning it on didn't change anything, and clicking Update by hand was still required every time. Automatic mode now really applies a pack update on its own once it's turned on and a pack folder is set (a launcher self-update still always has to be downloaded and installed by hand, the same as before). Also reworks the whole interface's look toward a lighter, glassier style — softer, more transparent cards and rounder buttons — with no changes to how updating, Play, or Settings actually work.
1.2.1: Fixes a serious bug in backup retention: backups were sorted by folder name, so after a version-number digit change the launcher could delete its newest backups the moment they were created while keeping older ones — exactly the backups a rollback would need. Retention now sorts by timestamp. Also fixes a case where a failed launcher self-update download could still show "Update complete" (the pack result and the launcher-download result are now reported separately and honestly). Visually, the main Update/Play decision button is now a blue glass pill in the Apple system-blue style; nothing about how updating, Play, or Settings work has changed.
1.3.0: The launcher is now called Corvus, and has the Corvus logo as its app icon. Your existing settings — pack folder, automatic update preference, backup retention — are carried over the first time you run it, and the old settings folder is left in place untouched as a safety net, so nothing is lost either way. Please note that because the app's name changed, installing this version does NOT replace the old one: a new Corvus app appears alongside the existing Glimpse Launcher, which you can delete by hand once you have confirmed Corvus opens with your settings intact. The download filenames change from glimpse-launcher-* to corvus-* for the same reason. Nothing about how updating, Play, or Settings work has changed.
1.3.1: Fixes a bug that stopped the launcher being set up at all: if you picked your mods folder in the folder chooser — which is exactly what the chooser's own title told you to pick — it was rejected with a message that read as though your mods were missing. Either folder now works: choose your Minecraft folder or the mods folder inside it, and the launcher works out the rest and shows you the exact folder it will install into. It also now looks for your Minecraft installation on startup and offers it, so most people no longer need to go hunting for the folder at all — it always asks first and never adopts a folder on its own. One thing unchanged: a mods folder that is completely empty is still not accepted, because a folder with nothing in it cannot be told apart from an unrelated folder of the same name.
1.4.0: A completely rebuilt interface. Corvus now has a sidebar instead of tabs, and the Home screen shows what it actually knows at a glance — the installed version, the latest one, when it last checked, and the exact folder an update would be written into — with a live view of what it is doing underneath. Settings is a proper settings screen rather than a row of plain controls. Nothing about how updating, Play or Settings work has changed, and your existing settings carry over untouched. Two practical notes: the interface is dark only for now, and the cross-platform jar is considerably larger than before (about 10 MB rather than 1 MB) because the new interface toolkit is bundled inside it — the native installers already included it, so their size barely moved. If you use the jar and would rather not download that each time, the native installer for your system is the better option.
1.5.0: Corvus can now update itself. From this version on you should not need to visit this site again: when a new Corvus is released it downloads it, checks it against the SHA-256 published here, replaces itself and reopens. It always asks first, even with automatic updates turned on — restarting the app while you are using it is not something it should decide on its own. If anything goes wrong the previous version is put back automatically: the new build has to actually start before the old one is discarded. Two honest limitations. On Linux the .deb needs administrator rights that Corvus cannot request, so it downloads and verifies the file and then shows you the exact command to run — it does not pretend to have installed it. On Windows the update reinstalls the MSI, which means Windows will show its usual permission prompt. This release also follows the site to its new address; if you are on 1.4.0 or earlier you need to download once from here by hand, because those versions are still looking for the old address and cannot be reached.
1.5.1: Fixes a bug that could leave your Minecraft unable to start. If you installed the mod pack by hand before pointing Corvus at the folder — which the guide tells you is fine — the first update added the new mod files but could not remove the old ones, because it had no record of what was already there. Two copies of the same mod stops the game loading. Corvus now recognises the pack's own files by name, so superseded ones are removed whether or not it has a record, and it checks afterwards that only one copy of each mod is left. Your own mods are never touched: only files matching the pack's exact naming are removed, everything is backed up first, and each removal is written to the log.
1.5.2: Corvus now reads the pack's name from what this site publishes, instead of having it written into the app. Until now it always said "Glimpse Alpha" on its main screen — which became wrong the moment the pack was renamed to "Alpha", and could only have been corrected by shipping a new launcher. It now follows the name published here, so a future rename needs no launcher update at all. Nothing about updating, Play or Settings has changed. This release also rewrites several log messages that were showing raw internal detail rather than a sentence — including one that reported a failure as simply "null", which told you nothing about what had gone wrong.
1.6.0: Corvus now speaks 13 languages, matching this site — Japanese, English, Spanish, French, Chinese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazil), Italian, Arabic, Russian, Indonesian, German and Turkish. Pick one from Settings; it takes effect the next time you open Corvus. Arabic displays right-to-left throughout. Nothing about how updating, Play or Settings works has changed.
1.7.0: Corvus can now adjust some of the same settings the in-game admin app can — mob spawn rates, the Plague Doctor's natural spawn, and similar knobs — from Settings → Solo Play Tuning. This is for singleplayer only: on a multiplayer server, the server admin's own settings are what actually apply, so this screen has no effect there. It needs pack version 2.5.1 or later to work — on an older pack it will say so plainly rather than showing nothing. Changes take effect the next time you start Minecraft.
1.8.0: Corvus can now show the changelog without leaving the app: a new Changelog page in the sidebar lists every release grouped by version, and opening one shows what changed. There is also a Website link at the bottom of the sidebar. Both follow whatever update address Corvus is set to, so a custom or mirrored address opens the matching site rather than the default one.
1.8.1: Fixes the Windows installer. Until now the .msi installed Corvus but created no Start-menu entry and no desktop icon, so the install genuinely succeeded and then left you nothing to click — a progress bar would flash and vanish, which looks exactly like a failed install. The installer now creates both, shows a real setup wizard instead of running silently, and installs per-user so it needs no administrator prompt (which also means Corvus can update itself, something a Program Files install could never do). macOS and Linux are unchanged. If you have the broken 1.8.0 installed, it is most likely sitting in C:\Program Files\Corvus and can be removed from Apps & features.
1.8.2: Stops Corvus asking you to update forever. Every 1.8.1 build reported itself as "1.8.0" no matter what it actually was, so it compared itself against the published 1.8.1, decided it was out of date, and offered an update — which installed another build that also said 1.8.0, so the offer came straight back. Taking 1.8.2 once ends the loop: 1.8.2 correctly reports 1.8.2. This affected Windows, macOS and Linux alike; macOS simply hit it first. The version now comes from the build itself rather than a number someone had to remember to edit, and the release pipeline refuses to publish a build whose reported version disagrees with the version it was built as.
1.8.3: Fixes Corvus never opening on macOS — it would appear in the Dock, bounce, and never show a window. 1.8.2 read your pack's mods folder, opening every jar in it, before it was allowed to draw the window; if that folder lives on an external or slow drive there was no limit on how long that took. The scan now happens in the background and the window opens straight away, with the Aureum row filling in a moment later. Verified by launching the built app with a real pack folder configured: the window appears and the scan is no longer on the drawing thread.
1.9.0: Corvus now looks like macOS System Settings: a sidebar with a search field and coloured icons, and every setting laid out as rounded groups of rows. General opens with your computer account's own name and picture — on macOS read from Directory Services (verified on the developer's Mac); on Windows from the account's FullName and the AccountPicture registry entry, and on Linux from the passwd entry and ~/.face or AccountsService — those two are written to the documented locations but have NOT been run on a real Windows or Linux desktop yet, and fall back to your login name and initials if nothing can be read. Update holds the pack, the app, Aureum, and the auto-update and backup switches; Play moved to General. Nothing about how updates are checked, verified or applied changed. Verified by photographing every pane from the built jar on macOS in English, Japanese and Arabic.
2.0.0:
The window itself is now glass. On macOS Corvus puts AppKit's own blurred material behind a transparent window, so your desktop shows through the app the way it does through System Settings — not a picture of blur, the real thing, updating as what is behind it moves. A new Glass section on General holds two controls: Liquid Glass, which turns it on and off, and Glass tint, which sets how dark the glass is, from Clear to Dark. Turning Liquid Glass off gives the solid dark window 1.9.0 had, and that is also what Windows and Linux get: the material is a macOS API, and no attempt is made to fake it elsewhere.

The rows and cards inside the window are glass too, and much clearer than they were. Their fill was measured off a reference the owner supplied rather than chosen by eye: each card now sits 0.020 white over what is behind it, against the reference's own 0.015 to 0.054, and the shadow that used to hang under every card is gone — three of the reference's four cards have none, and a shadow is what made them read as slabs floating above the window rather than as part of it. The card border is unchanged at 0.15; the reference measures 0.149, so it was already right.

Two things that were painted on top of the glass have been removed. Three wide sky-blue fields were being drawn over the real material, which is what made the window read as droplets rather than as a pane; they now appear only when Liquid Glass is off, where they are the opaque window's atmosphere and belong. The wide blue halo behind your account picture is gone as well.

Verified by photographing the running window over a flat neutral desktop, which is the only way to tell the app's own painting from the desktop showing through: with the glass on, the window's empty field is perfectly flat and the cards sit inside the reference's own range; with it off, the atmosphere returns as designed. The macOS, Windows and Linux installers for this version were built by CI on each of those systems, but only the macOS build has been run.
2.1.0:
Corvus can now install Cherry, the separate mod, and keep it up to date. Cherry has its own row on Update. The first install only ever happens when you press Download: Corvus fetches the Cherry package, checks its size and SHA-256, unpacks it into a temporary folder, checks every jar inside against the manifest — its size, SHA-256, mod id and version — and only then puts Cherry and the GeckoLib it needs into your mods folder, all together or not at all; if anything fails, the folder is put back exactly as it was. After that — and also for a Cherry you put in your mods folder yourself — new Cherry versions install automatically, even when Install updates automatically is off; that switch still governs the pack, the app and Aureum. GeckoLib is never downgraded: a copy that is already the same version or newer is kept. A package that carries a jar the manifest does not list, or another product's jar such as Aureum, is refused whole.

Installs into the mods folder now take turns: Cherry's and Aureum's installers share one lock, the Update pane never runs a pack update and a Cherry install at the same time, and quitting to apply a launcher update waits up to a minute for a running install to finish. The manifest's new cherry section is read leniently: if anything in it is wrong, Cherry is shown as not published and a line goes to the Log, while the pack and the app still update as before.

Verified by installing the real Cherry V1.0.0 package, from the manifest the website builds from that package, through this version's own code: both jars arrived byte for byte with nothing left behind, and the same manifest with one wrong digit in the package's SHA-256 was refused before anything was written. The Update pane was photographed from the built jar in English and Japanese with an installed Cherry. Not yet seen: the Download and Update buttons against the live website, and an automatic Cherry update actually running. The macOS, Windows and Linux installers for this version are built by CI on each of those systems; none of them has been run yet.
2.2.0:
The changelog can now show OUKA, Cherry, Alpha or Aureum. A row of brand buttons sits above it: choose one to read that brand's history, newest first, and "Open on the website" opens the same brand's page. OUKA shows its message for now. Corvus reads the list of brands from the website; if the list is missing or cannot be read, the changelog shows Alpha's history exactly as before and the reason goes to the Log. A brand whose history fails to load shows the failure and a Retry button, and the other brands still work.

Verified: all 587 tests pass, twice, including checks that the list of brands is read strictly and that a broken list falls back to Alpha. This version was photographed reading the website's new files from a local copy, once with each brand chosen first. Not yet seen: switching between brands by clicking in the running app, and the macOS, Windows and Linux installers, which are built by CI on each of those systems and have not been run yet.
2.3.0:
Every animation in Corvus is now a damped spring rather than a fixed duration, and they are all stepped on one clock that stops when nothing is moving. A motion you interrupt keeps the speed it already had instead of starting again, so nothing jumps under your hand. Buttons take 0.95 under the pointer and light up; the switch is jelly; the sliders are liquid; the glass is built in layers — a blurred, saturated backdrop, a veil, a lit edge and a highlight that follows the pointer.

Dialogs and Solo Play Tuning can now be thrown away. Each carries a grab bar, follows the pointer when pulled down and resists on a rubber band pulled the other way. What happens when you let go is decided by how fast you were moving over the last tenth of a second, not by how far the sheet has travelled: thrown down hard it leaves at the speed you threw it, let go gently it goes only if the momentum it still carries would carry it past two fifths of its own height, and otherwise it springs back. The window behind it stands back while it is up and comes forward again in step with your finger, so changing your mind costs nothing.

On macOS a capsule now hangs from the top of the screen, above the menu bar, on every Space, and lets every click that is not on it pass straight through. It has four shapes and morphs between them: the notch alone, a minimal capsule with the cover and a dancing waveform, a Now Bar with the title, artist and the controls, and a console with shuffle, repeat, a volume bar and your output device. A tap opens it, a long press or a downward swipe opens the console, and a swipe up, Escape or a click elsewhere folds it away. A new track surfaces the Now Bar for four seconds and it tucks itself back — unless your pointer is resting on it. It reads what Music and Spotify broadcast about themselves, which needs no account and no permission of any kind; Corvus does not sign in to anything. A switch on General ("Show the L Window") turns it off, and it is on to begin with.

OUKA and ASTRAEA join Cherry on Update: each has its own row, the first install is a button you press, and after that new versions install themselves. A package that carries a jar the manifest does not list is refused whole, and a dependency two brands share — GeckoLib — belongs to neither of them, so installing one never removes or downgrades the other's copy.

The changelog was showing its own mark-up. The history is written for the website, which renders it; Corvus was drawing it as plain text, so 206 lines of the published English history, spread across 15 of its entries, were showing tags around the words they were meant to emphasise. Those lines are now laid out properly, with the bold parts actually bold, and only the two marks the feed really uses are treated as mark-up — the entries document commands with angle brackets in them, and treating those as tags would have deleted the argument names from the instructions.

Verified: 729 unit tests pass twice, and two instruments drive the built application and check what it does rather than what it was asked to do — 80 claims on the window (including a stress test that lets nothing finish and then asks whether every value is still a number, still in range and exactly at rest) and 40 on the capsule. Both ran twice against the jar published here, with the display kept awake, and nothing failed in any of the four runs. A handful of claims came back as "cannot say" rather than as a pass: this machine was busy, and where a claim needs a quiet one the instrument refuses to judge it instead of calling it a pass. The load is written into the line. Not verified, and worth saying: nobody has thrown a sheet with a trackpad or seen the capsule's frosted backdrop on a screen, the media controls have never been sent to a real player, the volume and output device have never actually been set, there is no notched screen or Intel Mac here, and one thing measured and left unfixed — the moment a sheet arrives or leaves is drawn at 60 frames a second rather than 120, which predates this version and is the crossfade behind it, not the sheet. The macOS, Windows and Linux installers are built by CI on each of those systems. The macOS one was opened here and the app inside it run: it reports 2.3.0, opens its window and draws all four screens. The Windows and Linux ones have not been installed or run by anyone.
3.0.0:
Corvus is now Corvus Store: a store front for the studio's products, laid out the way the App Store is. A sidebar down the left has Discover, Mods, Library and Updates, and your computer account at the foot; a search field at the top searches the products by name (蕾, ノクチュア and アストレア find Tsubomi, Noctua and ASTRAEA) and by what they are. Discover is a column of big cards — the newest releases first, then every product — and pressing a card grows it into its full article; pull the article down, press Escape or press the cross and it shrinks back into the card it came from. Each product has its own page: icon, developer, the version, what it runs on, its languages, a description, What's New with a Version History of every release, and a table of facts. A number that is not published is shown as a dash, never guessed.

Pressing your account at the foot of the sidebar opens the one place where anything is set: Automatic Updates, the Minecraft folder mods are installed into, Language, Perch, Solo Play Tuning, and Export Diagnostic Logs, which saves what Corvus Store has written about itself to a file. There is no settings window and no log viewer. Automatic Updates is on unless you turn it off: with it on, Corvus Store keeps itself and the mods it installed up to date; with it off, nothing updates by itself. Alpha, which has ended, is no longer updated by Corvus Store at all — its last release turns the blocks it added into air, so nothing applies it for you.

The button on every card is the App Store's: GET becomes a ring with a stop square in it while the package downloads, with the speed and the time left under it, then OPEN — which opens the official Minecraft Launcher — and UPDATE when a newer version is out. Stopping a download deletes the partial file and leaves your mods folder exactly as it was. OUKA, Cherry and Aureum can be installed and updated from a card; Tsubomi, Noctua and ASTRAEA say "Coming soon"; Alpha, which has ended, shows the site's own notice and no download.

The window is flat: a black canvas, solid dark-grey cards with a hairline edge, blue for the one thing to press. The glass of 2.0 to 2.3 is gone, and on macOS only the sidebar lets the system's own translucent material show through.

The L Window is now Perch, and it is a different thing: a solid black capsule with continuous corners that floats just below the menu bar and needs no notch. It keeps out of sight while the app that is playing — Spotify or Music — is in front, and pops out with a spring the moment you leave it; tap it, or rest the pointer on it, and it opens into a control deck with the cover, title, volume, output and the transport buttons. Your hearts, and whether you had it switched on, carry over from the L Window. Perch is macOS only in this version.

The app, its installers and its update address are still called Corvus, so every installed copy can update itself from the same place.

Verified: 899 unit tests pass on every one of three clean builds, with the compiler set to refuse any warning. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages (118 checks each, English, Japanese and Arabic included) and run against the real update check with a manifest served from this machine (38 checks). The built application was driven in a real window twice: all 92 of the window instrument's claims held, none failed, none were undecided. Perch's own instrument, on the finished build: 46 or 47 claims held in each of five runs, none failed, and three in each could not be decided because the machine was busy (an earlier build of the same Perch code held 49 twice); one run in which the pointer of the person using the machine sat over the capsule is not counted. The macOS installer, built by CI, was opened here and the app inside it run: it reports 3.0.0, opens its window and draws all five screens (Discover, Mods, Library, Updates and Search). It is built for Apple Silicon Macs only. Not verified, and worth saying: Corvus Store replacing itself on an installed copy (the download, the checksum and the refusals are tested; the swap was not run); nobody has seen the sidebar's system material on a screen, felt Perch under a trackpad, seen it on a display with a notch, or pressed GET on a card for a first install; the Windows and Linux installers have not been installed or run by anyone; and the wording of the new badges, subtitles and the Perch switch in the twelve languages other than English (Japanese: Tsubomi's line is the studio's own) is a translation that nobody who speaks them has read.
3.0.1:
Corvus Store 3.0.1 is a small release with two changes.

The Updates page now works the way the App Store's does. It has no "Check for Updates" button and no line about when it last checked. It checks by itself when you open it (unless it checked a moment ago), every fifteen minutes while Corvus Store is open, and when you press Cmd+R (Ctrl+R on Windows and Linux). When two or more updates are waiting, an "Update All" button (すべてアップデート in Japanese) appears at the right end of the page's title and updates them one after another, Corvus Store itself last; with only one waiting there is no such button. It never starts a first install, it does not try an update twice, and if something else is writing into your mods folder it stops instead of refusing card by card.

The picture beside your name was a black disc in 3.0.0 — in the sidebar and at the top of the account sheet, for every account picture and every monogram. The ring that outlines the picture had lost its style when the old settings panels were removed, and a circle is filled black unless told otherwise. It is now a hairline and nothing else, and a picture with see-through pixels sits on the card's grey. That was a fault of 3.0.0, and nothing you did.

The official icons of OUKA, Cherry, Aureum, Tsubomi, Noctua and ASTRAEA, which came with 3.0.0, are unchanged. Everything else is 3.0.0.

Verified: 913 unit tests pass on each of two clean builds, with the compiler set to refuse any warning, and the two builds made byte-identical programs. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages (138 checks each, English, Japanese and Arabic included), including a check that reads the account picture pixel by pixel — with the 3.0.0 code it reads black, and with this one it reads the picture — and the Updates page: no check button, one check when it is entered, Update All appearing at two waiting updates and gone at one, and going through them in turn with Corvus Store last. It was run against the real update check with a manifest served from this machine (38 checks). The built application was driven in a real window twice: all 94 of the window instrument's claims held, none failed, none were undecided, including that Cmd+R starts one check and that opening Updates after a while starts one. Perch's own instrument, on this build: 47 claims held in each of two runs, none failed, and three in each could not be decided because the machine was busy (Perch is unchanged since 3.0.0). The macOS installer, built by CI, was opened here and the app inside it run: it reports 3.0.1, opens its window and draws all five screens, with no check button on Updates and the account picture showing; it is built for Apple Silicon Macs only.
Not verified, and worth saying: the fifteen-minute wait itself (the decision is tested, the timer is the system's); an Update All run against real downloads (the order and the stopping are tested with stand-ins; the installs it presses are the same ones GET and UPDATE press); a slow check is invisible, because the cards keep showing what they showed while one runs; Corvus Store replacing itself on an installed copy; the Windows and Linux installers, which nobody has installed or run; and the words "Update All" in the twelve languages other than Japanese, which nobody who speaks them has read.
3.0.2:
Corvus Store 3.0.2 is a small release with two changes.

Tsubomi can now be installed from the Store. Tsubomi is published as one jar rather than a package of several, and Corvus Store 3.0.0 and 3.0.1 did not know that shape, so its card said "Coming soon". The card now has a GET button like OUKA, Cherry, ASTRAEA and Aureum have. Pressing it downloads the jar, checks its size and SHA-256 against the site, and puts it in your mods folder; once it is installed, Tsubomi updates itself in place, and an installed copy is found by what the jar is, not by what the file is called. Tsubomi cannot run beside Alpha: its own jar says so, and Minecraft would refuse to start. So if your mods folder holds any Alpha module, the Store says so in one plain sentence that names the jars, and changes nothing. That applies to updates too.

The icons are the new ones. OUKA, Cherry, Aureum and Corvus Store itself now show the same icons as the website; they are the website's own files, not redrawn copies, and the big pictures on the Today cards of OUKA, Cherry and Aureum are the website's new banners. In a language that reads right to left the banner is arranged for it, with the emblem on the left and drawn as it is, not mirrored. The old marks are gone from the application, from the macOS, Windows and Linux installers' icons, and from the Today cards. One thing to know: the largest size inside the macOS icon is the 512 pixel logo enlarged, because 512 pixels is all the studio supplied.

Everything else is 3.0.1.

Verified: 933 unit tests pass, with the compiler set to refuse any warning, and two clean builds made byte-identical programs. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages (138 checks each, English, Japanese and Arabic included), and no icon, banner or preview in the program has the bytes of an old one (a test keeps the old marks out and holds the new ones to the website's files). It was run against the real update check with a manifest served from this machine (50 checks, 12 of them new for Tsubomi): with no Tsubomi block the card says Coming soon; with one it offers GET at 1.0.0 and does not install by itself; beside an Alpha module it refuses and leaves the folder unchanged; once installed it shows OPEN and updates itself to 1.0.1. The real Tsubomi 1.0.0 jar from this site went through the installer too: its thirteen Alpha module ids are found, it installs into a clean folder and is refused beside an Alpha module. The built application was driven in a real window twice: all 94 of the window instrument's claims held in each run, none failed, none were undecided. Perch's own instrument, on this build: 47 claims held in one run and 49 in the other, none failed, and three and one could not be decided because the machine was busy (Perch is unchanged since 3.0.0). The macOS installer, built by CI, was opened here and the app inside it run: it reports 3.0.2, its icon file is the one in the repository, and it draws all five screens with the new icons and a GET button on Tsubomi; it is built for Apple Silicon Macs only.
Not verified, and worth saying: Tsubomi in a real Minecraft client (nobody has run it there yet); a Tsubomi download from this site through a real Store window (the real jar went through the installer directly, and the check against the update code used a copy served from this machine); how the refusal dialog's long sentence is laid out; that sentence is in English in every language, like the other install failures; the Windows and Linux installers, which nobody has installed or run; and the Tsubomi words in the twelve languages other than English, which are the ASTRAEA wording with the name swapped and which nobody who speaks them has read.
3.0.3:
Corvus Store 3.0.3 adds Halia.

Halia, The Max Model, is now in the Store, first on the shelf, with a GET button. It is published as one jar, like Tsubomi, and is installed the same way: pressing GET downloads the jar, checks its size and SHA-256 against the site, and puts it in your mods folder; once it is installed, Halia updates itself in place. Read its page before you press the button in the game: Halia's orbital strikes destroy very large areas of a world for good, so back up your world first. Halia needs Minecraft 26.3, Fabric Loader 0.19.5 or newer, Fabric API 0.161.0+26.3 or newer and Java 25; for multiplayer it must be on the server too.

The installed app can now check itself. Running "Corvus --live-install-check <report file>" makes it install every mod the site publishes into scratch folders, with its own bundled Java, and write what happened to that file. It was written because a Windows 11 player could not get Tsubomi and nobody had the text of the error. Run on a Windows machine with the Windows installer installed, it installed Cherry, OUKA, ASTRAEA and Tsubomi from this site without a failure, so that report is not reproduced and nothing in the installer was changed for it. One known cause that is not a fault: Tsubomi is refused, on purpose, while any Alpha module is in the mods folder.

Everything else is 3.0.2.

Verified: 934 unit tests pass, and two clean builds made byte-identical programs. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages (145 checks each, none failed). It was run against the real update check with a manifest served from this machine (50 checks). The built application was driven in a real window twice: all 94 of the window instrument's claims held in each run. The real Halia 1.0.0 jar went through the installer with a manifest carrying its entry: it installs beside other mods and refuses nothing. The macOS installer, built by CI, was opened here and the app inside it run: it reports 3.0.3 and draws all five screens with Halia on the shelf; it is built for Apple Silicon Macs only.
Not verified, and worth saying: Perch's own instrument failed one claim once (the volume bar's swell under the pointer) while this machine was very busy and passed when repeated, and Perch is unchanged since 3.0.0; Halia has not been pressed in a real Store window against this site before this release; Halia on Windows, in multiplayer or beside the other mods in a real game; the Windows and Linux installers of this build, which nobody has installed by hand; eleven unit tests fail on Windows (helper scripts and wording written for macOS and Linux, none in the mod installer) and have not been sorted; and Halia's one-line description in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese, which nobody who speaks them has read.
4.0.0:
Corvus Store 4.0.0 is Corvus V4: your own server can now keep itself in step with the Store.

Corvus Agent is new. It is a small program that runs beside a Minecraft server you host yourself and makes that server's mods match what this site publishes, so players and server stop drifting apart. You list the mods the server runs in its config file. When it is asked to sync, it downloads what has changed, checks each file's size and SHA-256 against the site, and only then touches the server: it copies the mods folder aside, stops the server, replaces the files, starts the server and waits for it to answer. If the server does not come back, it stops it, puts the old files back and starts it again. It does not update while players are online unless you tell it how long to wait. It touches only the mods you listed, never the others in the folder. Download it from the Download page; the package holds the program, a setup guide and an example config. It needs Java 25.

Corvus Store has a new setting, Linked server, at the bottom of the account sheet. Switch it on, enter your agent's address and its token, and press Test connection. From then on, after the Store installs or updates a mod, it tells your agent to sync. Plain http is accepted only for this computer or your local network; for a server on the internet, put the agent behind https.

Everything else is 3.0.3.

Verified: 1,009 unit tests pass (core 431, Store 532, agent 46), and two clean builds made byte-identical programs. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages (146 checks each, none failed). It was run against the real update check with a manifest served from this machine (50 checks). The agent was run against a real Minecraft 26.3 Fabric server on a Mac: it installed Tsubomi, Cherry and Halia from this site into the running server and the server came back with all three loaded; it updated an older Tsubomi; with a start time limit set too short on purpose it stopped the half-started server, restored the previous files exactly and started it again; its listener refused a missing and a wrong token, started one sync for the right one, and ignored an address planted in the request. The Store's own client was run against the running agent. Every safety rule of the agent has a test that was shown to fail when the rule is broken.
Not verified, and worth saying: the built application was driven in a real window and no claim failed, but only one of the two runs could decide every claim (94 of 94); the other was cut short by a busy machine with 4 timing claims undecided. The player check was tested with a stand-in, not a real player. The agent has not been run on Linux or Windows, under systemd or Docker, or on a second machine behind a proxy. Nobody has pressed the Linked server controls by hand in a real window. The token is kept in plain text in the Store's settings file. The agent has no https of its own. The Linked server words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese were not read by speakers. The Windows and Linux installers of this build were not installed by hand.
4.1.0:
Corvus Store 4.1.0 adds one thing: Corvus Agent can be set up from the Store.

Corvus Agent is the small program that sits beside a Minecraft server you host yourself and keeps its mods in step with the Store. Until now it was a zip from the website and a command typed in a terminal. It is now the last entry on the Store's shelf. Press GET and choose your server folder: the Store downloads the agent, checks its size and SHA-256 against the site, puts it in that folder as corvus-agent.jar, and writes its configuration and two start scripts (start-with-corvus.bat, and .sh for Linux and macOS). It looks in the folder's mods and lists the Corvus mods it finds there, and it reads your server's own start command from the .bat or .sh you already use, so there is nothing to edit by hand. From then on you start the server with start-with-corvus: the agent checks for updates before the server starts and every ten minutes while it runs, stops the server with its own "stop" command when nobody is online, swaps the mods, starts it again, and puts the old files back if it does not come up. The Store itself never starts, stops or talks to your server.

A folder that is not a server folder is refused before anything is downloaded, and nothing is changed. An existing configuration is never overwritten, and a start script the Store did not just create is never edited: if you set the agent up by hand before, the Store tells you the one line to change. When a newer agent is published the entry shows UPDATE; updating replaces that one jar and touches nothing else. If the server is running and holds the file, the Store says so and changes nothing: stop the server, then press Update again.

Corvus Agent 4.1.1 comes with it. Its --init command now finds the mods in the folder too, and the package from the website is otherwise as before.

Everything else is 4.0.0.

Verified: 1,081 unit tests pass (460, 83 and 538 in the three modules), with the compiler set to refuse any warning. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages and every check passed. The installer was run on a copy of a real Fabric 26.3 server folder on macOS: it found the three mods there, read the server's command, and the server was then started with the script it wrote; the agent updated one mod before the first start and stopped the server with its world saved when asked to close. On a Windows machine in CI the agent's tests pass, including the ones that run a real child process.
Not verified, and worth saying: nobody has pressed the buttons in a real Store window yet, so the dialogs and the folder chooser have only been tested from code; nothing has been run on a real Windows server; the update has not been run against a published package; the "server is running" case was simulated; the words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese were translated plainly and have not been read by a native speaker. The entry's icon is the Corvus mark, not artwork of its own.
5.0.0:
Corvus Store 5.0.0 and Corvus Agent 5.0.0 take care of a Minecraft server you host yourself, so that you no longer have to.

Corvus Agent now runs the server for you. When an update is published it waits until nobody is playing, backs up the world, stops the server, swaps the mods, starts it again and checks that it answers; if it does not, it puts the old mods back and starts it again. It backs the world up on its own every six hours by default (keeping the newest seven), pausing the game's saving while it copies so the copy is never half-written, and it can put any of those backups back with one confirmation, taking a fresh backup first. If you use playit.gg it opens the tunnel once the server is up, and if playit is stopped it tries once to start it. Everything it does is written down.

Corvus Store has a new screen for this: Agents (Corvus Studio). The Dashboard shows the server, the tunnel, the backups and any update at a glance, with Start, Stop, Restart, Back up now and Update now. Activity lists what the agent did, in your language, and lets you restore a backup or read the logs. Settings let you turn automatic updates and automatic backups on or off, choose how often to back up and how many to keep, start the server when Corvus Store opens, keep it running when Corvus Store quits (the default), and open Corvus Store when the computer starts. Together that is: switch the computer on, and the server and the tunnel come up by themselves.

If you set the agent up with an earlier version, 5.0.0 picks up where it was. If the old agent is still running the server, Corvus Agent 5 does not start a second one; it says so, and takes over once the old window is closed. A start script that Corvus wrote is updated to the new agent; one you changed is left alone, and the Store tells you the one line to change.

Verified: 1,212 unit tests pass (474, 149 and 589 in the three modules), with the compiler set to refuse any warning. Corvus Agent 5 was run against a real Fabric 26.3 server on macOS: it started the server, took a backup through Corvus Store's controls (saving paused and resumed), installed an update in the order above, restored a backup after asking for confirmation, refused to start a second server while an Agent 4.1 ran the same folder and took over when it stopped, and shut everything down cleanly. On Windows (CI), the installed Corvus Store started the agent, the agent kept running after the Store quit, its controls answered, a second agent in the same folder refused to start, and the "open at start-up" switch wrote and removed the correct entry; the official playit installer was installed and its real output is what the agent reads.
Not verified, and worth saying: nobody has yet pressed the new buttons in a real Corvus Store window on Windows, or run a real Minecraft server on Windows with it; a playit account was never claimed here, so a live tunnel, the wording playit prints while running, and whether playit can be started without administrator rights on your PC are not confirmed (if it cannot, the Dashboard tells you); "open at start-up" was not tried through a real sign-in; the words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese were translated plainly and not read by a native speaker.
5.0.1:
Corvus Store 5.0.1 rearranges the Store.

The Mods section is now Arcade. At the top a large banner shows the models' own artwork in turn, with the model's line and its button; below it you can show all models, only the ones you have installed, or only the ones with an update. Top Models lists every released model, numbered, in this order: Halia, OUKA, ASTRAEA, Cherry, Tsubomi, Noctua and Aureum. Noctua runs on Palworld servers, so the Store does not install it; its button opens its page on the website. It used to be listed as Coming soon, which was wrong: it has been out since 4 October. The retired Alpha follows underneath.

The new Work section holds Corvus Agent: its card to get, update or open it, and under it Corvus Studio (Dashboard, Activity, Settings) for the server it looks after. It takes the place of the Agents section, so there is still the same number of sections. Corvus Agent is no longer listed among the models; an update to it is offered on its card in Work.

Everything else is 5.0.0.

Verified: the unit tests pass (594, 474 and 149 in the three modules) with the compiler set to refuse any warning, including new tests that hold the order, keep Corvus Agent out of Arcade and check every language says Arcade and Work. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages, and the new Arcade and Work screens were looked at in English, Japanese and Arabic (mirrored).
Not verified, and worth saying: the banner's crossfade, hover and press have not been seen in a real window; nothing new was run on Windows; the words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese were translated plainly and have not been read by a native speaker.
5.0.2:
Corvus Store 5.0.2 and Corvus Agent 5.0.1 carry out the end of ASTRAEA's service.

ASTRAEA ended its service on 16 October 2026. In the Store it is now archived: it moves to the end of Arcade, just before Alpha, it is no longer numbered in Top Models or shown in the banner, and it can no longer be installed or updated. Its button opens the notice on the website. A copy already on your computer is left as it is.

Corvus Agent 5.0.1 removes ASTRAEA from the servers it looks after, on its first sync on or after 23 October 2026. Before then it changes nothing; Corvus Studio's Dashboard shows the date. On the day, it takes a world backup first, stops the server, moves the ASTRAEA jar into .corvus-retired (it is not deleted), starts the server again and checks that it answers; if it does not, everything is put back. This happens even when automatic updates are off. OUKA and every other mod stay exactly as they were. Removing ASTRAEA removes its blocks, items and worlds (the Moon, Mars and the station) from your world, so back up any world you want to keep; the backup the agent takes is in .corvus/backups. To get the removal, update Corvus Agent from its card in Work.

Everything else is 5.0.1.

Verified: the unit tests pass (601, 481 and 159 in the three modules), including new tests for the removal date, the move, the roll-back and that no other file changes. On a real Minecraft 26.3 server with OUKA 1.6.2 and ASTRAEA 1.5.4, the agent changed nothing before the date; on the date it made the world backup (with ASTRAEA's worlds in it), moved the jar, and the server started without ASTRAEA while the other six mods were byte-identical. The Store was drawn without a window in all 13 languages with ASTRAEA archived, and was looked at in a real window. Corvus Agent 5.0.0 and Corvus Store 5.0.1 read the new website data without trouble.
Not verified, and worth saying: the Dashboard's date line and the ASTRAEA notice in the Store have not been seen in a real window; the new words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese have not been read by a native speaker; until you update, Corvus Store 5.0.1 still offers ASTRAEA, and Corvus Agent 5.0.0 does not remove it.
5.0.3:
Corvus Store 5.0.3 and Corvus Agent 5.0.2 follow the website to its new address.

The Corvus website has moved to iroponcopin.github.io/corvus-dev. The Store and the Agent now read updates there. If your Store or Agent was set to the previous address, it switches to the new one by itself the first time it starts; nothing needs to be changed by hand. The name of the website is now simply Corvus.

Everything else is 5.0.2 and 5.0.1.

Verified: the unit tests pass (603, 481 and 160 in the three modules), including new tests that a saved setting with the previous address is moved to the new one, in the Store and in the Agent, and that every link the Store opens points to the new site.
Not verified, and worth saying: the new address was checked from the published site after release, not before it; earlier versions of the Store and the Agent keep working because the previous address still forwards the update information for now.
5.1.0:
Corvus Store 5.1.0 and Corvus Agent 5.1.0 remove ASTRAEA for good, add a difficulty above Hard, and bring the recipes into the Store.

ASTRAEA is now removed everywhere. Corvus Agent 5.1 removes it from every server it looks after, straight away, including servers whose agent settings never listed it. It takes a world backup first, stops the server, moves the ASTRAEA jar into .corvus-retired (it is not deleted), starts the server again and checks that it answers; if it does not, everything is put back. Corvus Store 5.1 does the same on your PC: ASTRAEA's jar leaves your mods folder and is moved into .corvus-retired inside the pack folder, and the Store tells you once. Removing ASTRAEA removes its blocks, items and worlds from a world, so keep the backup if you need it.

XHard is a new difficulty for servers, above Hard. Hostile mobs have 1.5× health and attack, move a little faster and notice you from further away. It is not hardcore: dying works as on Hard. Choose it in Corvus Studio (Work, Settings, Difficulty): the agent installs the small Corvus XHard mod on the server and switches it on. Players need nothing new. When you first start Corvus Agent 5.1, it sets the server to XHard once; you can change it back at any time.

The Store has a new section, Album: every recipe for Halia, OUKA, Cherry and Tsubomi, with a search and the crafting grid, the same as on the website. It is kept on your computer, so it still opens when you are offline.

Whitelist sync: Corvus Agent can add players to the server's whitelist from the Corvus SI approval queue on Discord. Enter the service address and its secret in the Whitelist sync card in Corvus Studio. The secret is never shown again or written to a log.

Verified: 1,298 unit tests pass (490, 188 and 620 in the three modules). On a real Minecraft 26.3 server on macOS with ASTRAEA installed but not listed, Corvus Agent 5.1 made the world backup, moved the ASTRAEA jar, installed Corvus XHard, switched to XHard, and the server started without ASTRAEA while the other mods stayed byte-identical; a zombie's health went from 20 to 30 and its attack from 3 to 4.5, and back when XHard was turned off. The Album, the Difficulty card and the Whitelist sync card were looked at in a real Store window.
Not verified, and worth saying: nothing was run on Windows; whitelist sync was not run against the real Corvus SI service; the Store cannot tell whether Minecraft is running when it moves the ASTRAEA jar (on Windows, if the game holds the file, nothing is moved and the Store tries again next time); the words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese were translated plainly and have not been read by a native speaker.
5.1.1:
Corvus Store 5.1.1 and Corvus Agent 5.1.1 keep themselves up to date, and a retired model now leaves players' computers only after their server has let it go.

Corvus Agent now updates itself. When a new version is published, the agent downloads it, checks it, and waits until no player is online; then it stops the server cleanly, replaces itself, starts again and brings the server back. The previous copy is kept next to it as corvus-agent.jar.bak. If the new version does not start, the old one carries on. You can turn this off with the autoUpdateAgent setting.

Corvus Store now updates the Corvus Agent on the same PC by itself, with no click: if the Store set the agent up, it replaces the agent when a new version is out and restarts it when no player is online. With players online it waits for the next check.

A retired model is removed from players' computers only after their server has removed it, or on the removal date published on the website, whichever comes first. In Corvus Store 5.1.0 ASTRAEA left players' mods folders at once, while servers whose agent had not been updated still asked for it, so players could not join ("ASTRAEA not installed"). Corvus Store 5.1.1 waits for the server.

Fixes: an agent started in a console window now restarts itself if the new version fails to start, and its timer is stopped before the switch.

What to do once: nothing, if Corvus Store on that PC set the agent up. Otherwise press Update once on the Corvus Agent card (or replace corvus-agent.jar by the 5.1.1 jar and restart the agent). From 5.1.1 on the agent updates itself.

Verified: 1,321 unit tests pass (497, 198 and 626 in the three modules). On a real Minecraft 26.3 server on macOS, Corvus Agent 5.1.1 updated itself to a newer test version, in the background and in a console window, and Corvus Store 5.1.1 replaced and restarted an Agent 5.0.2 it had set up, which then removed ASTRAEA while every other mod stayed byte-identical.
Not verified, and worth saying: nothing was run on Windows; going back from Agent 5.1 to 5.0.2 needs the difficulty line removed from the agent settings by hand; when the Store replaces the agent it keeps no .bak copy; the words in the eleven languages other than English and Japanese were translated plainly and have not been read by a native speaker.
5.2.0:
Corvus Store 5.2.0 and Corvus Agent 5.2.0 add Pro, a difficulty above XHard.

On Pro, hostile mobs have 2.8 times the health and attack, bosses included: the Wither, the Ender Dragon, the Elder Guardian and the Warden. The Ender Dragon's bite and breath, the Wither's skulls and the Warden's sonic boom also hit 2.8 times harder. The Warden's health stops at 1024, the game's own limit. Everything else is as on XHard, and it is not hardcore.

To celebrate Halia V1.3, every server runs on Pro until 19 November 2026 (UTC). There is nothing to do: Corvus Agent switches the server by itself, and Corvus Studio shows the end date. After that, admins can choose any difficulty again; the server stays on Pro until they do. XHard is unchanged.
5.5.0:
Corvus Store 5.5.0 and Corvus Agent 5.5.0 bring a new Store design, a Tools page, Corvus AI 5.5 Chat and new strength and spawn-rate settings for servers.

The Store has been redrawn from scratch: a new layout with frosted glass surfaces for the sidebar, cards, sheets and buttons.

Tools is a new page, directly under Arcade. It installs Aureum, the performance mods Sodium and Iris for shader support, and 7 shader packs: Complementary Reimagined, Complementary Unbound, BSL, Photon, Solas, MakeUp Ultra Fast and Bliss. There is no setup: it finds your Corvus pack folder, or the standard Minecraft folder, by itself, and a shader pack adds Sodium and Iris first when they are missing. Every file is checked against its hash before it is installed.

The Tools page shows "This computer": the system, processor, memory and graphics card with its VRAM. It is read on your computer only and is never sent anywhere.

On Windows, when a shader pack is installed on a graphics card with 12 GB of VRAM or less, the Store warns that high-end shader packs may use a lot of GPU memory or drop frames, and asks whether to proceed.

Corvus AI 5.5 Chat is free. Under the input it says: Corvus AI 5.5 actively researches unfamiliar topics to answer your questions. Please double-check important information.

Difficulty becomes two settings in Corvus Studio. Strength of hostile mobs (health, attack, armor and aggression), 10 tiers: Low −25%, Medium ±0%, Hard +25%, Xhard +50%, Pro +75%, Max +100%, Ultra +150%, UltraFast +200%, UltraCore +250%, Ultimate +300%. Spawn rate of hostile mobs, 7 tiers: Low −25%, Medium ±0%, High +25%, Xhigh +50%, Max +75%, Ultra +100%, UltraFast +200% (4x). Medium is the default for both.

During the event, until 19 November 2026 (UTC), the minimum strength is Pro: tiers below Pro cannot be chosen, and a lower setting is raised to Pro. Pro and everything above it stay selectable.

Pro is now +75% (×1.75) instead of ×2.8. The Warden is never made stronger than Pro, and at UltraCore and Ultimate the Wither's health stops at Minecraft's limit of 1024.

The old solo-play tuning has been removed.

Corvus Agent and Corvus Store keep each other updated: both move to the same version by themselves.
